Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Functional Synergy between the Munc13 C-terminal C1 and C2 domains" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Randy Schekman (Senior editor) and three reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some relatively minor remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below:

The reviewers would like to thank the authors for addressing the concerns raised previously. Based on their new findings, the authors have changed the conclusions from their studies. Rather than suggesting a synergism between the synaptotagmin and Munc13 C2 domains, they now suggest synergism between the C2B and C2C domains of Munc13-1 and that Munc13-1 may bridge V- and T-liposomes in a calcium independent manner (Figure 6—figure supplement 5). The authors' new data correlating the activation of SNARE fusion with (at least in part) a role in the specific clustering/docking of V- and T-liposomes by Munc13 significantly clarifies the primary message of the paper and is a result that will be of general interest.

Comments:

1) The manuscript remains very long. Considering the revised conclusions, the authors are encouraged to take a fresh look and examine if all the data are really essential for the key conclusions.

2) There are some supplementary figures that are actually quite important (e.g., Figure 4—figure supplement 4, and Figure 6—figure supplement 5). Please restrict supplementary figures to repeat experiments, raw data, and non-essential experiments.

3) A general comment regarding all figures that compare lipid and content mixing results (Figures 4, 5, 7, 8, 9 and numerous supplemental figures): both types of experiments (lipid mixing and content mixing, respectively) are normalized differently: for lipid mixing 1% BOG is added and the resulting fluorescence intensity value is used for normalization; whereas for content mixing, it is the maximum value for each group of conditions in the particular panel. So, 100% content mixing could actually correspond to substantially fewer vesicles undergoing content mixing than vesicles undergoing lipid mixing. A suggestion would be to change all figure panel titles from "lipid mixing" to "relative lipid mixing" and "content mixing" to "relative content mixing", and to change all the y-axis labels from "Fluorescence (% of max)" to "Fluorescence (arbitrary units)". Another comment: ensemble experiments cannot determine what fraction of vesicles that undergo lipid mixing also undergo content mixing.

4) Figure 4—figure supplement 4C. We appreciate that the authors have performed DLS measurements to address the concern that the large increase in content mixing upon calcium addition could be due to a calcium-dependent docking/clustering effect. However the presence of large vesicles might dominate in the intensity autocorrelation functions shown. Percent Intensity plots (similar to those shown in Figures 2 and 6) should also be provided for Figure 4—figure supplement 4C.

5) Figure 4—figure supplement 4C was only done for the soluble Syt1 C2AB fragment. If at all possible, please also perform the DLS experiments also with full-length Syt1. The reason is that there is much less lipid mixing in these experiments prior to calcium addition than for the experiments with the soluble Syt1 C2AB fragment (compare Figures 7 and 8).

6) Figure 9: It is perhaps possible that there could be compensating factors in neurons that do not show a large phenotype for the DN mutant of Munc13. Nevertheless, if the author's model of calcium-independent bridging of T and V-vesicles by C1C2BMUNC2C is correct (Figure 6—figure supplement 5), why would calcium binding to the C2B domain of Munc13 have such a large effect? Please discuss.

7) Figure 6—figure supplement 5: While the preference for the C1C2B domain for the T-vesicle membrane can be explained by the presence of DAG and PIP2 in that membrane, what is the mechanism that C2C would only interact with the V-vesicle membrane?

8) Figures 2 and 6: why does C1C2BMUN cluster V-vesicles, whereas C1C2BMUNC2C does not? This question is also related to the Discussion section, paragraph five. Please provide an explanation why the C2C domain would favor trans-interactions with V-vesicles.

9) Subsection “Simultaneous evaluation of lipid and content mixing”, paragraph two": "A problem…". Actually, synaptic vesicles are acidic, so the property of sulforhodamine to produce an acidic interior of the proteoliposomes is not necessarily a problem. Moreover, the lack of leakiness under such conditions is desirable. In any case, it is good that the authors confirmed the content mixing results with the different content mixing assay by Zucchi and Zick. Thus, there is really no "problem" with the sulforhodamine content mixing assay.

10) Figures 1D and E: the effect of the different lipid compositions (PIP2 and DAG) appears to be much more pronounced in the presence of NSF/SNAP/Munc18, although C1C2BMUN is present in both experiments.

11) Discussion, paragraph seven: in addition to Lee and Kyoung, please also cite the improvements of this assay by Diao et al. (eLife 2012); Lai et al. (eLife 2014). Another comment: the single vesicle content mixing assay by Kyoung et al. (2011); Lai et al. (2014) allows discrimination between effects that are due to docking vs. due to fusion probabilities in addition to the improved time resolution offered by such single vesicle assays.

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Functional Synergy between the Munc13 C-terminal C1 and C2 domains" for further consideration at eLife. Your revised article has been favorably evaluated by Randy Schekman (Senior editor) and a Reviewing Editor.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below:

We thank the authors for their thoughtful considerations of the concerns raised previously. However, the Reviewing Editor has two remaining concerns:

1) Related to Point 9, the authors write:

"A potential concern with the use of sulforhodamine B fluorescence de-quenching to monitor content mixing in these bulk reconstitution experiments is that de-quenching can also arise from liposome leakiness. We attempted to perform experiments where both liposome populations are loaded with sulforhodamine B to assess how much of the de-quenching arises from leakiness (Yu et al., 2013). However, we were unable to observe lipid mixing in these control experiments. Since the solutions of high sulforhodamine B concentrations trapped in the liposomes are highly acidic (pH about 2), which may underlie the lack of lipid mixing, we attempted to increase the pH of these solutions to 5.5 or 7.4 before trapping them into the liposomes, but at both pH values the liposomes were strongly leaky."

Their observation of lack of lipid mixing when both vesicle populations are filled with sulforhodamine B is strange, considering that the authors observed efficient lipid mixing when only one class of vesicles is filled (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Moreover, Kyoung et al., 2011 and Diao et al. 2012 observed both lipid and content mixing using their sulforhodamine B content mixing method, with only an extremely small fraction of leakage (0.01% of the docked vesicles). Could the problems be related to differences in reconstitution methods, rather than an issue with the sulforhodamine method per se?

This Reviewing Editor also would like to point out that the pH of the interior of the synaptobrevin/synaptotagmin vesicles ("donor" vesicles) is likely more neutral rather than pH 2 when using the published reconstitution protocol (Kyoung et al. Nat Protoc 8(1):1-16, 2013): the initial protein/lipid/detergent solution uses a detergent concentration that is at the CMC (OG ~ 30 mM), so vesicles do not yet form at this stage. This solution is then injected on a Cl-4B column that has been pre-equilibrated with vesicle buffer (pH 7.4, without sulforhodamine B), followed by elution with vesicle buffer (pH 7.4, again without sulforhodamine B) (Kyoung et al. Nat Protoc 8(1):1-16, 2013). Vesicles are forming on the column in a time course of several minutes as the detergent concentration decreases. One would expect that the pH of the interior of the column rapidly reaches 7.4.

In any case, as the authors point out, the alternative PhycoE-Biotin/Cy5-Streptavidin content mixing assay produces similar results (Figure 3—figure supplement 3). However, as written, the second paragraph of subsection “Simultaneous evaluation of lipid and content mixing” may come across to the casual reader as if there is something wrong with the sulforhodamine B content mixing method. Since this is a rather technical issue that distracts from the main messages of this paper, and that may be related to differences in reconstitution methods, the authors may wish to consider deleting this entire paragraph. In the future, perhaps the authors may wish to investigate a variety of content mixing assay jointly with other groups who have developed these assays for a more technical publication.

2) Point 11, related to the sentence starting "Approaches that allow faster measurements [e.g. single vesicle assays (Lee et al., 2010; Kyoung et al., 2011); will be required to test this prediction. " It is not just the faster time resolution that is important for future studies. The single vesicle-vesicle lipid/content mixing assay by Kyoung et al. 2011, Diao et al., 2012 et al. (but not the assay by Lee et al., 2010) can distinguish between effects due to docking, lipid mixing and content mixing on a 100 msec time scale for each individual vesicle pair. In addition to the improved time resolution, the discrimination between effects due to docking and/or fusion will be important for future studies. The authors may wish to consider making the discussion of the relevant publications clearer.

results.result: The C1, C2B, and C2C domains of Munc13-1 exhibit functional synergy, helping to bridge vesicle and plasma membranes to facilitate SNARE complex assembly by the MUN domain, thereby coordinating synaptic vesicle docking, priming, and fusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7 and C107 are supported by converging evidence from reconstitution experiments (showing enhanced fusion with C1C2BMUNC2C vs. shorter fragments), liposome-clustering assays (demonstrating membrane bridging), and electrophysiological data (rescue experiments). The synergy between domains is demonstrated through multiple experimental approaches showing that the full C1C2BMUNC2C fragment is significantly more active than individual components.

results.result: Munc18-1, Munc13-1, NSF, αSNAP, and SNAREs form a 'primed state' that includes assembled trans-SNARE complexes, does not fuse spontaneously, but is ready for fast fusion upon Ca2+ binding to the Munc13-1 C2B domain.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9 and C134-C136 are well-supported by reconstitution data showing substantial lipid mixing but minimal content mixing before Ca2+ addition (C132-C133), with fast content mixing after Ca2+ (Figure 9). The requirement for these specific proteins (C186) and correlation with physiological priming (C187-C188) provide strong support for this primed state model.

results.result: The Munc13-1 C2C domain is critical for neurotransmitter release, as C1C2BMUNC2C is much more efficient than C1C2BMUN in facilitating Ca2+-dependent fusion, while MUN and MUNC2C fragments alone are inactive.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 are strongly supported by fusion assays (Figures 4, 9) showing dramatic enhancement with C1C2BMUNC2C compared to shorter fragments. This is corroborated by electrophysiological rescue experiments (C138-C139, C144-C145, Figure 10) showing ~50% rescue with C1C2BMUNC2C versus minimal rescue with shorter fragments, demonstrating the critical role of the C2C domain in vivo.

results.result: C1C2BMUNC2C preferentially bridges V-liposomes to T-liposomes in a Ca2+-independent manner, suggesting that Munc13s play a role in bridging synaptic vesicles to the plasma membrane, which contributes to docking and facilitates MUN domain activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C104 are supported by DLS data (Figure 6) showing that Ca2+-free C1C2BMUNC2C does not cluster V-liposomes alone but efficiently bridges V- to T-liposomes. The bimodal distribution experiments (C100-C101) and correlation with enhanced fusion efficiency (C103, C156) provide strong evidence for this bridging mechanism and its functional significance.

results.result: Ca2+ binding to the Munc13-1 C2B domain is critical for efficient content mixing in the primed state, as the D706N,D711N mutation strongly impairs content mixing while not affecting Ca2+-independent lipid mixing.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C122 are directly supported by experimental data (Figure 9E,F) showing that the D706N,D711N mutation in the C2B domain abolishes Ca2+-dependent content mixing while preserving lipid mixing. This selective effect, combined with DLS data showing similar clustering for WT and mutant (C123-C126), demonstrates that Ca2+ binding to the C2B domain is specifically required for the transition from the primed state to full fusion.

results.result: Munc13-1 C1C2BMUN strongly stimulates SNARE-dependent lipid mixing in a Ca2+-, DAG-, and PIP2-independent manner by binding simultaneously to two PS-containing membranes, thereby favoring SNARE complex assembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 are supported by NBD de-quenching assays (Figure 1B) showing strong lipid mixing stimulation that is SNARE-dependent (impaired by Syb-cd) and Ca2+-independent. The membrane bridging mechanism (C60-C61) is supported by DLS data (Figure 2) showing efficient clustering of PS-containing vesicles by C1C2BMUN, with PS being the main determinant (C58).

results.result: Syt1 C2AB selectively enhances content mixing but not lipid mixing in reconstitutions with C1C2BMUN, Munc18-1, NSF-αSNAP, and Ca2+, indicating that Syt1 plays a specific role in membrane fusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 are directly supported by simultaneous lipid and content mixing assays (Figure 3) showing that Syt1 C2AB strongly enhances content mixing while having minimal effect on lipid mixing. This selective enhancement (C72) demonstrates a specific role for Syt1 in completing membrane fusion (C73), consistent with prior single-vesicle studies.

results.result: In the presence of NSF-αSNAP, lipid mixing requires C1C2BMUN, Munc18-1, and Ca2+, and is stimulated by DAG and PIP2, exhibiting properties similar to neurotransmitter release. NSF-αSNAP ensure that fusion proceeds through the Munc18-1-Munc13-dependent pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 and C51 are supported by lipid mixing data (Figure 1C) showing efficient fusion only when both C1C2BMUN and Munc18-1 are present with NSF-αSNAP, with Ca2+-dependence. The dependence on DAG and PIP2 (C48, Figure 1E) and correlation with physiological properties (C52) are well-documented. The mechanistic role of NSF-αSNAP (C152-C153) is supported by their known activity in disassembling syntaxin-1-SNAP-25 heterodimers.

results.result: Membrane fusion in reconstitutions with VSyt1-liposomes depends strictly on both Munc18-1 and Munc13-1 C1C2BMUNC2C, exhibits tight Ca2+-dependence, and is markedly impaired by removal of the C1-C2B region or C2C domain, correlating with requirements for neurotransmitter release in neurons.
results.evaluation: Claim C118 is directly supported by fusion data (Figure 9C,D) showing complete abolition of fusion when either Munc18-1 or C1C2BMUNC2C is absent. The Ca2+-dependence (C148) and impairment by domain removal (C149-C150) are demonstrated by Figures 9B,D and Figure 10, respectively. The correlation with in vivo requirements (C119) strengthens the physiological relevance of these findings.

results.result: In rescue experiments, the C1C2BMUNC2C fragment rescues ~50% of EPSC amplitude compared to WT Munc13-1, while MUN, MUNC2C, and C1C2BMUN fragments show only minimal rescue despite higher expression levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C139 are directly supported by electrophysiological data (Figure 10A,B) showing robust rescue with C1C2BMUNC2C versus minimal rescue with shorter fragments. Similar results for the readily-releasable pool (C140) strengthen this conclusion. The observation that all fragments are expressed at higher levels than WT (C141) rules out expression level as a confounding factor, and the minimal rescue by shorter fragments (C142) demonstrates their functional deficiency.

results.result: C1C2BMUN efficiently clusters PS-containing vesicles but not plain liposomes, with PS being the main determinant for clustering activity. Inclusion of synaptobrevin, DAG+PIP2, or syntaxin-1, and Ca2+ have minimal effects on clustering.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C56 are directly supported by DLS data (Figure 2A,B) showing dramatic particle size increases only for PS-containing vesicles. The lack of major effects from other lipids/proteins (C57) and Ca2+ (C59) is demonstrated by Figures 2B-F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The conclusion that PS is the main determinant (C58) is well-supported, though the authors appropriately note they cannot rule out small contributions from other factors.

results.result: C1C2BMUNC2C alone stimulates fusion between V- and T-liposomes strongly but in a Ca2+-independent manner, with efficiency similar to Syt1 C2AB in the presence of Ca2+. Munc18-1 slightly increases this efficiency, while Syt1 C2AB enhances fusion with the less efficient C1C2BMUN fragment.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 are supported by fusion data (Figure 5A,B) showing strong Ca2+-independent fusion with C1C2BMUNC2C alone, comparable to Syt1 C2AB-stimulated fusion. The modest enhancement by Munc18-1 (C88) and lack of Syt1 effect with C1C2BMUNC2C (C90) versus enhancement with C1C2BMUN (C91) are clearly demonstrated in Figure 5, showing differential effects based on fragment efficiency.

results.result: C1C2BMUNC2C is more efficient in liposome clustering than C1C2BMUN, with the C2C domain potentially increasing liposome affinity. C1C2BMUNC2C clusters V-liposomes only with Ca2+ but clusters T-liposomes regardless of Ca2+, suggesting preferential bridging of V- to T-liposomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 are supported by DLS (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and co-floatation data (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) showing enhanced clustering and potentially increased affinity with C1C2BMUNC2C. The differential clustering of V- versus T-liposomes (C95-C96, Figure 6—figure supplement 3) and the inference of preferential bridging (C97) are well-supported by the experimental data, though the mechanism remains to be fully elucidated.

results.result: At 20°C, C1C2BMUNC2C clusters T-liposomes but not V-liposomes in the absence of Ca2+, with V-liposomes requiring Ca2+ for clustering. A bimodal distribution is observed when C1C2BMUNC2C is added to mixtures of plain and T-liposomes, while only clustered vesicles are detected in V+T mixtures without Ca2+.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99 are directly supported by DLS data at 20°C (Figures 6A-D) showing differential clustering behavior. The bimodal distribution (C100, Figure 6F) demonstrates the ability to distinguish clustered from non-clustered populations. The observation that only clustered vesicles are detected in V+T mixtures (C101, Figure 6G,H) provides strong evidence for preferential bridging, as all vesicles appear to be incorporated into clusters.

results.result: VSyt1-liposomes fuse efficiently with T-liposomes in a Ca2+-independent manner, with C1C2BMUN slightly increasing fusion efficiency and Munc18-1 having no marked effect. However, NSF-αSNAP abolish fusion, which then requires Munc18-1, C1C2BMUN, and Ca2+.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111 are supported by fusion data (Figure 8A,B) showing efficient Ca2+-independent fusion with VSyt1-liposomes, consistent with prior work (Stein et al., 2007). The abolition by NSF-αSNAP and restoration by Munc18-1+C1C2BMUN+Ca2+ (C112-C113, Figure 8C,D) demonstrate that membrane-anchored Syt1 behaves similarly to soluble Syt1 C2AB in these reconstitutions, validating the use of both approaches.

results.result: Fusion assays with VSyt1-liposomes in the presence of NSF-αSNAP, Munc18-1, and different Munc13-1 fragments yield similar results to those with soluble Syt1 C2AB, with C1C2BMUNC2C being much more active than C1C2BMUN. Content mixing requires Ca2+ despite lipid mixing occurring before Ca2+ addition, and is very fast upon Ca2+ addition.
results.evaluation: Claim C114 is supported by comparison of Figures 9A,B with Figures 4C,D showing similar patterns with membrane-anchored versus soluble Syt1. The Ca2+-requirement for content mixing despite pre-Ca2+ lipid mixing (C115-C116) and fast fusion upon Ca2+ addition (C117) are clearly demonstrated in Figure 9, consistent with the primed state model and showing that membrane anchoring of Syt1 does not fundamentally alter the fusion mechanism.

results.result: In 8-fold diluted fusion reactions with WT C1C2BMUNC2C, much liposome clustering occurs within 3 min before Ca2+ addition, with little change 1 min after Ca2+ and moderate increases as the reaction completes. The D706N,D711N mutant shows efficient clustering after 3 min that does not increase further, suggesting Ca2+ binding to the C2B domain might enhance bridging but cannot alone explain the dramatic Ca2+-induced enhancement of content mixing.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C126 are supported by DLS data (Figure 9—figure supplement 3E,F) showing clustering kinetics for WT and mutant C1C2BMUNC2C. The similar clustering behavior between WT and mutant (C126) despite their dramatically different fusion efficiencies (C121-C122) supports the inference that Ca2+-enhanced bridging alone cannot explain the fusion enhancement (C127-C128), pointing to additional Ca2+-dependent mechanisms in the fusion process.

results.result: Removal of DAG, PIP2, or both from T-liposomes causes considerable impairments of fusion with C1C2BMUNC2C. A small amount of residual Ca2+ (likely ≤1 μM) appears sufficient to trigger fusion, with this sensitivity attributable to the C2B domain; residual Ca2+ might arise from the purified C1C2BMUNC2C fragment.
results.evaluation: Claim C82 is directly supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 showing impaired fusion without DAG/PIP2. The inference about low Ca2+ sufficiency (C83) is supported by experiments showing similar fusion with 100-120 μM added Ca2+ as with 600 μM (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), though the authors appropriately note that more accurate Ca2+-dependence assessment requires further research. The attribution to the C2B domain (C84) is reasonable given its known Ca2+-binding properties.

results.result: The D706N,D711N mutation disrupts content mixing but not Ca2+-independent lipid mixing, correlating with the observation that efficient content mixing with WT C1C2BMUNC2C requires Ca2+ while substantial lipid mixing occurs without Ca2+. Quantification shows lipid mixing at 300s is 28.9% of maximum while content mixing is only 3.3%.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C131 describe the correlation between mutation effects and WT behavior, supported by data in Figures 9E and 9A,C,E. The quantification (C132-C133, Figure 9—figure supplement 2) provides strong numerical support for the distinction between lipid and content mixing, demonstrating that the primed state allows substantial lipid mixing but minimal content mixing before Ca2+ addition, with the mutation specifically disrupting the Ca2+-triggered content mixing step.

results.result: Removal of DAG, PIP2, or both from T-liposomes causes increasingly stronger impairments of lipid mixing in experiments with C1C2BMUN, Munc18-1, and NSF-αSNAP, but has much milder effects on lipid mixing stimulated by C1C2BMUN alone without NSF-αSNAP.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49 are directly supported by experimental data (Figure 1D,E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D) showing differential effects of DAG/PIP2 removal depending on the presence of NSF-αSNAP. This demonstrates that the complete reconstitution system (with NSF-αSNAP) has stronger dependence on these lipids than the simpler system, consistent with the more physiological properties of the complete system.

results.result: The extent of lipid mixing with C1C2BMUN is comparable to that caused by Syt1 C2AB in the presence of Ca2+. Munc18-1 has only a small stimulatory effect on lipid mixing and does not enhance the stimulation caused by C1C2BMUN.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44 are supported by data in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing similar lipid mixing levels for C1C2BMUN and Syt1 C2AB+Ca2+, with Munc18-1 showing minimal effects alone or in combination with C1C2BMUN. This establishes that C1C2BMUN has potent membrane-bridging activity comparable to the well-characterized Syt1 C2AB system, but through a Ca2+-independent mechanism.

results.result: Efficient lipid mixing in the presence of NSF-αSNAP requires C1C2BMUN, Munc18-1, and Ca2+, while Syt1 C2AB does not markedly affect lipid mixing under these conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 are directly supported by experimental data (Figure 3A,C) showing that all three components (C1C2BMUN, Munc18-1, Ca2+) are required for efficient lipid mixing with NSF-αSNAP present, and that Syt1 C2AB addition does not significantly enhance lipid mixing. This contrasts with the strong effect of Syt1 C2AB on content mixing (C70), highlighting the selective role of Syt1 in completing fusion rather than initiating membrane merger.

results.result: Syt1 C2AB has no marked effect in experiments with C1C2BMUNC2C, likely because this fragment is already highly efficient in promoting fusion. In the absence of Ca2+, C1C2BMUNC2C is more active than C1C2BMUN in promoting lipid mixing but does not stimulate content mixing.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 are supported by data in Figure 4 showing no additional effect of Syt1 C2AB with C1C2BMUNC2C, with the explanation that the fragment is already maximally efficient being reasonable. The differential effects in the absence of Ca2+ (C80-C81) are clearly demonstrated in Figure 4, showing that C1C2BMUNC2C can promote lipid mixing but not content mixing without Ca2+, consistent with the formation of a hemifusion or primed intermediate.

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive background on established knowledge about neurotransmitter release machinery, including the roles of SNAREs, NSF-SNAPs, Munc18-1, Munc13s, and Synaptotagmin-1, as well as the domain structure and known functions of Munc13-1.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 and C11-C38 represent established knowledge in the field, supported by extensive prior literature as indicated by the numerous citations. These claims provide essential context for the current work and are appropriately cited. While these are not novel findings of this manuscript, they are accurately represented and provide the necessary foundation for interpreting the new results.

results.result: The reconstitutions recapitulate many key features of synaptic vesicle fusion and are consistent with prior studies on Munc13 function in docking and priming. The model is consistent with the architecture of Munc13s and related tethering factors, and the requirements for primed state formation correlate with physiological findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C146 and C161-C168 describe the consistency of the reconstitution system with physiological observations and prior studies. The correlations with in vivo requirements (C187-C188) and structural/functional relationships to tethering factors (C164-C165) are well-supported by the data and citations. These claims appropriately contextualize the findings within the broader field and strengthen the physiological relevance of the reconstitution approach.

results.result: The proposed model assumes NSF-αSNAP disassemble syntaxin-1-SNAP-25 complexes and Munc18-1 binds closed syntaxin-1, with membrane bridging creating a cage-like environment for SNARE assembly. The primed complex likely includes C1C2BMUNC2C and Munc18-1, consistent with their known binding to SNARE complexes and prior studies suggesting post-assembly roles.
results.evaluation: Claims C157-C160 and C189-C195 describe model assumptions and speculations about the primed complex composition. While these are reasonable inferences based on known protein interactions (C190-C191) and consistent with prior studies (C192-C194), they remain speculative (C189, C195) as the exact composition and structure of the primed complex have not been directly determined. The model is plausible and consistent with available data, but requires further experimental validation.

results.result: Various speculative claims about mechanisms, including the membrane bridging activity contributing to docking, the presence of multiple membrane binding sites in Munc13 fragments, potential lipid-binding by the C2C domain, and possible mechanisms for Ca2+-dependent fusion enhancement.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64, C105-C106, C143, C173-C177, and C196-C198 represent speculative interpretations and mechanistic proposals. While these are reasonable hypotheses based on the experimental data, they are explicitly acknowledged as speculative by the authors (using terms like "might," "may," "likely") and require additional experiments for validation. The speculation is appropriate for a Discussion section but does not constitute supported results.

results.result: Various observations about Ca2+ effects on clustering, lipid mixing behavior in different conditions, limitations of the reconstitution system, and comparisons with physiological studies on Munc13-2 mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C183 and C185 describe experimental observations about Ca2+ effects and lipid mixing mechanisms, supported by the data presented. Claims C199-C208 discuss comparisons with prior physiological studies and limitations of the current work. These are appropriately qualified statements that acknowledge uncertainties (C201-C202, C204-C205) and provide context for interpreting the results. The observations are well-supported, though some interpretations remain speculative.

results.result: Prior reconstitution studies showed Munc13-4 promotes Ca2+-dependent docking of V- to T-membranes, though it is unclear how this relates to Munc13-1 activity due to different Ca2+-binding properties. Synaptic vesicle docking and priming occur before Ca2+ influx, and correspondingly, C1C2BMUNC2C can bridge membranes without Ca2+.
results.evaluation: Claim C169 accurately cites prior work on Munc13-4. The uncertainty about the relationship to Munc13-1 (C170) is appropriately acknowledged given the different Ca2+-binding properties of their C-terminal C2 domains. The statement about the timing of docking/priming (C171) is established knowledge, and the correlation with C1C2BMUNC2C bridging activity (C172) is well-supported by the DLS data in Figure 6.
